analysis.one_liner: Strengthens enforcement and penalties for laws banning pay discrimination between men and women.
analysis.headline: The Paycheck Fairness Act drew 170 cosponsors in the House but was referred to subcommittees and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it easier for women to win equal-pay lawsuits by raising the penalties employers face, allowing wage-discrimination cases to proceed as class actions, letting workers recover compensatory and punitive damages, and protecting employees who ask about or discuss wages from retaliation. It would also narrow the excuses employers can use to justify pay gaps, require them to show any pay difference is truly job-related, and direct the government to collect pay data by sex, race, and national origin to help enforce the law. Separate sections would fund training, research, voluntary employer self-evaluations, and an award for good actors.
analysis.who_benefits: Women who are paid less than men for comparable work gain stronger tools to sue and larger recoveries when they win. Workers of both sexes gain protection against being punished for asking about or discussing wages. Families relying on every paycheck gain if discriminatory pay gaps are closed.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the stakes for violations of the Equal Pay Act by adding compensatory and punitive damages, and lets courts award expert fees to employees who win [S2][S3].
Allows wage-discrimination cases to be brought as class actions and extends the time limit for joining one, so workers with small individual claims can combine together [S2][S3].

Protects employees and applicants from retaliation for inquiring about, discussing, or disclosing wages, which the bill's findings say is necessary for workers to recognize and enforce their rights [S2][S3].

Requires employers to show that any pay difference rests on a job-related factor actually applied reasonably, and blocks employers from raising women's pay only to cut other women's wages later; it also extends coverage to job applicants [S2][S3].
Directs the EEOC to issue regulations collecting employer pay data by sex, race, and national origin so the government can better detect and enforce pay discrimination [S2][S3].
Funds training, research, a national summit, voluntary job-evaluation guidelines, technical assistance, and an award recognizing employers who close pay gaps without lowering men's wages [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers pay more when they violate equal-pay rules: higher damages, class-action exposure, and new pay-data reporting requirements. Businesses bear costs of litigation and compliance even when they act in good faith; some of that cost may be passed on in prices or hiring.

drawbacks.text: The bill's tougher remedies cut both ways: expanded compensatory and punitive damages, class actions, and a stricter burden on employers' defenses would raise litigation costs, and honest supporters would acknowledge that some disputes would turn on hard judgments about whether factors like experience or prior salary are genuinely job-related [S2][S3].

The bill directs the EEOC to write regulations requiring employers to report pay data by employees' sex, race, and national origin, a recurring compliance burden the bill itself says should be balanced against the burden on employers [S2][S3].
Portions of the bill are soft: the research, summit, award, and voluntary guidelines sections carry no mandate on any employer and would have modest effect on their own [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill is a real remedy upgrade for workers who can prove pay discrimination, paid for by higher litigation and compliance costs on employers. The enforcement sections carry the weight; the voluntary programs and award are trimmings. Whether the added litigation burden is worth it depends on how often employers would change pay practices to avoid lawsuits rather than fight them. The bill died without a hearing or vote, so its practical design was never tested in legislative negotiation.

outcome.mechanism: The House speaker's ally in charge of labor policy sent it to two subcommittees, and it sat there until the two-year Congress ended without a hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on June 30, 1999 with more than 100 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S3][S5].
The bill reached 170 cosponsors — 168 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 1 Republican [S4].
On August 6, 1999 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations and the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where the action record ends [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the bill's action history, and the 106th Congress ended January 3, 2001 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers are better off: they never faced the higher damages, class-action exposure, retaliation ban, or pay-data reporting the bill would have imposed. Workers with equal-pay claims gained nothing.

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and recruited more than 100 original cosponsors including the House minority leader.

for.name: 168 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it 168 of its 170 supporters from their party.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to two subcommittees and never held a hearing or markup during the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Held the committee chairmanships and floor schedule in the 106th Congress
against.what_they_did: Allowed the bill to die in subcommittee without a vote, despite its 170 cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly all Democratic — 168 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 1 Republican among 170 cosponsors — while the Republican-run committee took no action on the bill [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Employers subject to the Equal Pay Act (businesses of all sizes)
industries.note: The bill would raise employer liability with compensatory and punitive damages, class actions, and expert fees, narrow the defenses employers can use for pay gaps, ban retaliation for discussing wages, and require pay-data reporting [S2][S3]. Its interest in blocking the bill runs against workers seeking equal pay.

industries.industry: Employers who have closed internal pay gaps
industries.note: The same bill creates voluntary evaluation guidelines, technical assistance, and a national award recognizing employers who pay women fairly without cutting men's wages [S2][S3].
